hints: Remember what family 2,4-DNPH is famous for testing, think about the specific C=O group it looks for.
Look closely at option D and spot its simple ketone group, then compare it to the alkene, ester and acid in the other structures.
Recall that carboxylic acids and esters do not give this test even though they contain C=O, so pick the true aldehyde or ketone.
walkthrough:
**Recall what 2,4-DNPH tests for**

This is a classic qualitative test you must know by heart. 2,4-DNPH gives a yellow-orange precipitate only with aldehydes and ketones.

Reaction idea:
$$\text{R}_2\text{C=O} + \text{H}_2\text{N-NH-C}_6\text{H}_3(\text{NO}_2)_2 \rightarrow \text{R}_2\text{C=N-NH-C}_6\text{H}_3(\text{NO}_2)_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$
That orange solid is the 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazone.

**Sort the four functional groups**

Look at what each ring actually contains. A is cyclohexene, an alkene with $\text{C=C}$ and no oxygen at all.

B is a cyclic ester (a lactone) with $\text{-COO-}$, C is a carboxylic acid with $\text{-COOH}$, and D is cyclohexanone with a simple ketone $\text{C=O}$.

**Apply the selectivity rule**

Here is the key trap. Not every $\text{C=O}$ counts. Carboxylic acids, esters, acyl chlorides and amides do NOT give a precipitate with 2,4-DNPH.

Only the true ketone in D reacts, so D is the one that forms the yellow-orange precipitate.

options.A: Incorrect. This is cyclohexene, an alkene. It has a C=C bond but no carbonyl group, so it gives no reaction with 2,4-DNPH. Students sometimes confuse any unsaturation test with this carbonyl test.
options.B: Incorrect. This is a cyclic ester (lactone). Although it contains C=O, esters do not react with 2,4-DNPH to give the hydrazone precipitate. This is a common trap of thinking any C=O will work.
options.C: Incorrect. This is cyclohexanecarboxylic acid. Carboxylic acids contain C=O but do not give a positive 2,4-DNPH test. Only aldehydes and ketones do.
options.D: Correct. This is cyclohexanone, a cyclic ketone with a free C=O group. Ketones undergo condensation with 2,4-DNPH to form the yellow-orange 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazone precipitate.
